clue.text: One holding up other road users

definitions.text: One holding up other road users

blocks.clueFragment: One holding up other road users
blocks.note: surface reading: a slow driver or broken-down vehicle causing a tailback
setter's reading: holding up means robbing at gunpoint, as old mounted robbers did to travellers on the road

explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding up' reads as delaying traffic; the setter means an armed robbery of coach passengers, the trade of a figure from old English roads.
explanation.definitionFit: A highwayman was a mounted robber who stopped travellers on public roads and demanded their valuables.

clue.text: Premature ejaculation initially upsetting – maybe it’s the French letters

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of each word is kept
in a down clue, to upset something is to tip it over so its top ends at the bottom
maybe suggests one possible version of the letters, so they can be rearranged

blocks.note: the first letters of the two words
taken as written, apostrophe dropped
les is the French plural form of 'the'

explanation.surface: A smutty joke: an embarrassing bedroom mishap, with 'French letters' (British slang for condoms) as the punchline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French letters' is British slang for condoms, and the surface leans on it; in fact 'the French' gives LES and 'letters' alone is the definition. EP + IST + LES makes EPISTLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Epistles are formal written letters, the word used for the New Testament letters of Paul and others.

clue.text: Minister a bore about his subject

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: a pest is a nuisance or tiresome person
RI is religious instruction, the school subject a minister would teach

explanation.surface: A clergyman is a crashing bore when he goes on about his favourite topic.
explanation.walkthrough: RI stands for religious instruction, an old British name for the school subject; 'his' ties that subject to the minister.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest is a member of the clergy who ministers to a congregation, so minister is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Guy called out for drinks

indicators.note: something called out is spoken, so we go by what the word sounds like

blocks.note: to guy someone is to mock or tease them

explanation.surface: A man shouts an order for a round of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a noun for a man, but it is the verb meaning to ridicule, which is TEASE.
explanation.definitionFit: Teas are cups of tea, a common hot beverage, so the plural noun matches drinks.

clue.text: Half of street parking removed, snaps seeing constraints

indicators.note: half of a word keeps just one of its two halves, here the front half
something removed is taken away, so a letter is struck out

blocks.note: the first half of the word: three of its six letters
snaps are photographs
P is the standard sign for parking

explanation.surface: A council takes away half the parking on a street, and residents feel hemmed in by rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half of street parking removed' reads as one complaint about lost parking spaces, but it splits into two separate instructions with a comma's worth of pause after 'street'.
explanation.definitionFit: Strictures are restrictions or limits imposed on someone, so the plural noun is a synonym of constraints.

clue.text: See 21 Across
Cut in pub brawl in Mexican neighbourhood

indicators.note: cut means shortened, so the tail letter is lopped off

blocks.note: a bar is a pub
a riot is a violent disturbance

explanation.surface: Someone gets a cut during a bar fight in a Mexican district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like a wound from the brawl; it is an instruction to trim the final letter of the word for brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrio is the Spanish word for a district or quarter of a town, used for Hispanic neighbourhoods in Mexico and the US.

clue.text: Picked up small bird

indicators.note: picked up as heard, as a radio picks up a signal, so the sound matters

blocks.note: minor means small; in British speech the final R is silent

explanation.surface: Someone lifts a tiny bird from the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' suggests lifting by hand; it means heard. The match relies on a non-rhotic British accent where MINOR drops its R.
explanation.definitionFit: The myna is a starling-family songbird from Asia, famous for mimicking human speech.

clue.text: Continuing past main road turning right? Absolutely!

indicators.note: turning round means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, with 1 read as I
an exchange of agreement: 'Right?' answered by the emphatic 'Perfect!'

explanation.surface: A driver asks whether to carry on past the motorway and turn right, and gets an emphatic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's main motorway, from London to Leeds, with the digit read as the letter I. 'Right' does double work: part of the driving direction and the question answered with an emphatic 'Perfect!'.
explanation.definitionFit: The imperfect is the grammatical tense for actions that were ongoing in the past, such as 'I was walking'.

clue.text: Over here taking puff, it’s exhilarating

indicators.note: taking in something means holding it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a shout to get attention, as in 'Hey!'
a puff is a piece of promotional praise, like an advertisement

explanation.surface: Someone calls a friend over to share a smoke and finds it thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puff' suggests smoking; here it is publicity puffery, a promotional notice, and 'Over here' is the shout used to get attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Heady means intoxicating or thrilling, describing something that excites the senses like a strong drink.

clue.text: German takes road east and puts his foot down

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: Hans is a typical German man's name
ST is the abbreviation for street
E is the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A German driver turns onto an eastbound road and accelerates.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords often stand a common first name in for a nationality, so 'German' gives a typical German man's name rather than an abbreviation like G.
explanation.definitionFit: To put your foot down on the accelerator is to speed up, which is what someone who hurries does.

clue.text: Wrongly flippant about ancient region

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: ill as an adverb means badly or wrongly
airy means light-hearted and dismissive

explanation.surface: Someone is wrongly dismissive about an old historical region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning', linking flippancy to the region; it actually turns the word for flippant round.
explanation.definitionFit: Illyria was a classical region on the eastern Adriatic coast, roughly the western Balkans, later a Roman province.

clue.text: Set aside vote to sack leader

indicators.note: sacking the leader means dismissing the one at the front, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: a ballot is a vote

explanation.surface: A party sets aside a vote on getting rid of its leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a leadership challenge; in fact BALLOT just loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot is to assign or earmark a share of something for a particular purpose or person.

clue.text: Put right over what reactionary branch of mathematics?

indicators.note: a reactionary wants to go backwards, so the letters run in reverse
over can mean covering on both sides, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: to put something down is to set it
a Tory is a right-winger, a member of the UK Conservative Party
eh? is a request to repeat something, like 'what?'

explanation.surface: Someone asks how to correct a reactionary branch of mathematics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' and 'reactionary' look like a political pair, but only 'right' gives letters, the name of the British right-wing party; 'reactionary' just turns the word for 'what?' round.
explanation.definitionFit: Set theory is the field of mathematics that studies collections of objects and is a foundation for most of the subject.

clue.text: Joiner Snug’s first key tip – act differently

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter only
done differently means arranged another way, so the letters change order

blocks.note: the first letter of the name
the three words taken as letters

explanation.surface: Snug the joiner from A Midsummer Night's Dream gets a tip to play his part differently.
explanation.walkthrough: Snug is the joiner (carpenter) among Shakespeare's amateur actors, which makes 'Joiner' look like a character note; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sticky tape holds things together, so it literally joins items, a playful reading of a carpenter's job title.

clue.text: Previous times OK – runs during training steady

indicators.note: during means within a span, so one piece is placed inside another
training reshapes something, so these letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: yes and OK both signal agreement
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
taken as written

explanation.surface: An athlete's past training sessions were fine, with steady runs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' and 'training' build a jogging picture; R for runs is the cricket scorecard abbreviation, and it joins the other letters before they are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Yesterdays, as a plural noun, means days gone by or past eras, so it matches earlier times.

clue.text: Card rejected, sisters got angry on being detained – apology noted

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run backwards
an angry state is a disturbed one, so these letters are stirred up
someone detained is held inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a SIM card in a phone
the two words taken as letters
re means on or concerning

explanation.surface: A card is returned, and the sisters lose their temper at being held up, so an apology is sent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apology noted' means a noted (famous) apology: the 1934 Cole Porter song in which a maid conveys her mistress's regrets at missing lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss Otis Regrets is a well-known Cole Porter song whose whole lyric is a polite excuse for an absence.

clue.text: Rock band’s origin occasionally embellished

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is kept
something embellished is dressed up and altered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A rock band's backstory has been dressed up now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock band' reads as one phrase about music, but 'Rock' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsidian is a glassy black volcanic rock formed when lava cools very fast.

clue.text: Cast! She finally got callback regarding American Beauty

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter only
to cast is to throw or mould, so these letters are thrown into a new shape
the tail of this word, back, means in the opposite direction, so letters run from end to start

blocks.note: taken as written
its last letter
to cite is to call or summon, as a witness to court

explanation.surface: An actress auditions, gets a callback and is cast in the film American Beauty.
explanation.walkthrough: The film title and audition words build a casting story; 'callback' splits into 'call' and 'back', and 'American' explains the spelling without the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Esthetic is the American spelling of aesthetic, meaning concerned with beauty and its appreciation.

clue.text: Foreign seamen’s applications kept upfront – they’ll all be handled the same

definitions.text: they’ll all be handled the same

indicators.note: upfront means at the very front, so only the opening letter of each word counts
something foreign is strange and unfamiliar, so the letters take an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: An immigration office keeps visa applications from foreign sailors at the front, promising equal treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handled' is slang for named (a handle is a name), so the definition means people who all have the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Namesakes are people or things sharing one name, and a handle is informal for a person's name.

clue.text: Very few spotted?

definitions.note: measly is an adjective meaning meagre; 'very few' describes a meagre number

blocks.note: first meaning: pitifully small in amount or number
second meaning: covered in spots, as with the disease measles

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second, literal sense: having measles, the disease that brings a spotty rash.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means contemptibly small, and in its original sense describes skin marked with the rash of measles.

clue.text: Become a total bore, might you say?

definitions.text: Become a total bore, might you say?

blocks.note: surface reading: turn into a completely tedious person
setter's reading: bore said out loud is boar, a wild pig, so becoming a total boar means turning entirely into a pig

explanation.walkthrough: 'Might you say' flags the sound pun: a total boar is a whole pig, and the idiom for doing something completely is built from exactly that picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to do something thoroughly and without holding back, and literally pictures becoming an entire pig.

clue.text: Have a good laugh at bull that’s cute?

blocks.note: bull (short for bullshit) and guff both mean nonsense
aw is the cooing exclamation at something sweet

explanation.surface: Someone laughs heartily at a bull that looks adorable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bull' suggests the animal; it is the slang for nonsense, GUFF.
explanation.definitionFit: To guffaw is to laugh loudly and heartily, the verb for a big belly laugh.

clue.text: Still escorting Desperate Dora, a very old date

indicators.note: someone desperate is in a frantic state, so the letters are thrown about
to escort is to accompany closely, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: still and yet both mean nevertheless
taken as written

explanation.surface: An old man is still taking Desperate Dan's sister Dora out on dates.
explanation.walkthrough: Desperate Dan is a cowboy in the British comic The Dandy, so 'Desperate Dora' looks like a name; 'Desperate' is the anagram signal. 'Year dot' is a British idiom for a very long time ago.
explanation.definitionFit: The year dot is informal British slang for the very distant past, as in 'since the year dot'.

clue.text: Why worry about alien?

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: the letter Y is pronounced 'why'
ado is fuss or bother

explanation.surface: Someone asks why we should fret about an extraterrestrial.
explanation.walkthrough: A letter's name can stand for the letter itself, so 'Why' gives Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Yoda is the small green Jedi master in Star Wars, a member of an unnamed non-human species.

clue.text: Ground with different entrance nearer the action

indicators.note: a different entrance means the way in changes, so the first letter is swapped for another

blocks.note: Anfield is Liverpool FC's stadium

explanation.surface: A sports ground gets a new gate that brings fans closer to the play.
explanation.walkthrough: Anfield is the home ground of Liverpool football club; change its first letter to I. The definition reads 'infield' as an adverb, as a fielder playing close to the batter.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket and baseball, infield means the area close to the batter, so a fielder there is close to the play.

clue.text: Going over the top, Romeo’s tackling very hard

indicators.note: in a down clue, going over means flipping end over end, so the letters run the other way
to tackle is to grab hold of, so one piece clasps another

blocks.note: the top is number one, written NO plus 1 read as I
the first letter of Romeo, which is also the NATO phonetic alphabet word for R

explanation.surface: A footballer goes in over the top of the ball, and Romeo is making a very hard tackle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over the top' looks like a foul tackle; 'the top' is number one, NO I, which is turned round with R inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron used as an adjective means extremely firm or unyielding, as in an iron will or an iron grip.

clue.text: Passed out moving closer to Bermuda Triangle

indicators.note: the closing letter of the place name is moved to a new spot, so the order changes

blocks.note: cards passed out to players are dealt

explanation.surface: Someone fainted on approaching the Bermuda Triangle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bermuda Triangle' reads as one place; 'closer to Bermuda' is its last letter A, which moves from the middle of DEALT to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek capital letter delta is shaped like a triangle, and river deltas are named for that shape.

clue.text: Don very deficient in self-regard? F-------!

indicators.note: deficient in means lacking, so a letter is missing

blocks.note: a don is a university teacher, a professor
vanity is excessive regard for oneself
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: An academic with very little self-esteem blurts out an expletive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' is the British word for a university lecturer, not the verb meaning to put on. The definition is the starred-out swear word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A word printed as F followed by dashes is a censored obscenity, which is an example of bad language.
